pronunciation_note: Pronounced 'o' in modern Japanese, though written with the kana を (wo)

definitions.explanation: Marks the direct object of a transitive verb—the thing that receives the action. {本|ほん}を{読|よ}む (read a book), ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べる (eat rice/a meal).
Marks the space through which movement occurs with verbs of motion. {道|みち}を{歩|ある}く (walk along the road), {空|そら}を{飛|と}ぶ (fly through the sky), {橋|はし}を{渡|わた}る (cross the bridge).

Marks the starting point or place from which one leaves with verbs like {出|で}る (leave), {卒業|そつぎょう}する (graduate from). {家|いえ}を{出|で}る (leave the house), {大学|だいがく}を{卒業|そつぎょう}する (graduate from university).

predicates_requiring.description: Common transitive verbs that take を for their object

departure_verbs.example: {大学|だいがく}を{卒業|そつぎょう}する
{故郷|こきょう}を{離|はな}れる

particle_contrasts.explanation: With potential verbs, が often replaces を (emphasizing ability rather than object)

examples.wo_example: {日本語|にほんご}を{話|はな}す

examples.ga_example: {日本語|にほんご}が{話|はな}せる

key_points: Potential forms can take either が (ability) or を (object)
が emphasizes the ability; を emphasizes the object being acted upon
Some speakers prefer を with potential forms in modern Japanese

particle_contrasts.explanation: For verbs of motion, を marks the path traversed; に marks the destination

examples.wo_note: を marks the space moved through

key_points: を with motion verbs = path/space traversed

fixed_patterns.meaning: centered on, with... as the focus
fixed_patterns.example: {東京|とうきょう}を{中心|ちゅうしん}に{活動|かつどう}する
fixed_patterns.example_english: operate with Tokyo as the center

fixed_patterns.example: {友達|ともだち}を{通|とお}じて{知|し}り{合|あ}った
fixed_patterns.example_english: got to know each other through a friend

examples.japanese: {水|みず}を{飲|の}んでください。
{友達|ともだち}と{映画|えいが}を{見|み}た。
examples.english: I watched a movie with a friend.

examples.japanese: {毎日|まいにち}{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}しているので、{少|すこ}しずつ{上手|じょうず}になってきた。
examples.english: Since I study Japanese every day, I've gradually been getting better.

examples.japanese: {角|かど}を{曲|ま}がってください。
{公園|こうえん}を{走|はし}っている{人|ひと}がいる。
examples.english: There are people running through the park.

examples.japanese: {空|そら}を{飛|と}ぶ{鳥|とり}を{見|み}ていると、{自分|じぶん}も{飛|と}びたいと{思|おも}う。
examples.english: When I watch birds flying through the sky, I wish I could fly too.

examples.japanese: {大学|だいがく}を{卒業|そつぎょう}した。
{会社|かいしゃ}を{辞|や}めました。
{彼|かれ}は{故郷|こきょう}を{離|はな}れて{都会|とかい}に{出|で}たが、{毎年|まいとし}お{正月|しょうがつ}には{帰|かえ}っている。
examples.english: He left his hometown for the city, but he goes back every New Year.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using を instead of が with predicates like {好|す}き, {分|わ}かる
common_mistakes.explanation: These predicates require が, not を

common_mistakes.mistake: Using に instead of を for path traversed
common_mistakes.explanation: When moving THROUGH a space, use を

notes: を is exclusively used as a grammatical particle—it doesn't appear in any other words in modern Japanese. In casual speech, を is sometimes dropped: ご{飯|はん}{食|た}べた (ate a meal). The three main uses are: (1) direct object, (2) space traversed with motion verbs, (3) point of departure with leaving verbs.
